title: Take the Trip
author: Dr. Andrea Nimaroff
summary: Developmental scientist and mother Andrea Nimaroff answers a question many parents quietly carry: is it okay to leave your small children at home and take a trip? Her answer is yes, regardless of the reason and probably regardless of the child's age. She grounds it in research on early environmental predictability, including a Columbia study showing that predictable caregiver behavior supports infants' statistical learning, and argues that what children learn comes from patterns repeated daily rather than from occasional events. The central pattern she wants children to absorb is that parents always return, and a weekend away is one more concrete rehearsal of leaving and coming back. She also argues that parents' own needs, friendships and marriage matter, and that a responsive parent includes being responsive to oneself. She acknowledges the fair objection that this could excuse inattentive parents, but notes that such parents are unlikely to be reading long essays on the subject.
points: Children build expectations from patterns of experience repeated over time, so one trip is far less significant than the thousands of ordinary daily interactions that make up the relationship.
The key lesson in every separation is that caregivers always return, and each reunion reinforces that a separation does not mean a relationship has disappeared.
Parenthood makes it easy to treat your own health, friendships and marriage as permanently secondary, but a responsive parent has to be responsive to their own needs as well.
Nimaroff separates what research can support (consistency, predictability) from what it has not studied, admitting that no one has measured outcomes of a parent's quick birthday trip.
The essay speaks to parent anxiety with a calm reframe: attentive parents already do more than they credit themselves for, and strong bonds can withstand a little time apart.
quotes: Anyone who has traveled anywhere with children deeply understands the distinct difference between a vacation and a trip.

Becoming a parent can make it surprisingly easy to treat your own needs, wants, health, friendships, and even your marriage as secondary to everything else, and dismiss them as less important factors you’ll prioritize one day when your children are older, sleeping better, or just generally require less of your entire energy reserve.
One of the most consistent themes in this work is that children learn strongly from patterns of experiences over time.
What we do infrequently is not nearly as significant for learning or development as what we do repeatedly. An occasional trip is not the same as a prolonged or unpredictable in and out absence.
Your relationship with your child is not built in singular moments, it happens over thousands of ordinary interactions.
Each reunion is another opportunity for children to learn that a separation doesn’t mean a relationship has disappeared.
Part of building strong bonds is knowing they can withstand a little time apart, and that our connections with our children support both their independence and our own.
